questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A comparison organised by a held-constant question
questions.learningObjective: identify a comparison organised by theme
questions.stem: An essay compares two invented novels by holding one question constant across both, asking what a character owes a person they have wronged, and it answers that question once for each book. What has the essay organised itself by?

options.text: By theme, since the question is held fixed and each book is read through it, so what is compared is two answers to one problem rather than two books in general
By date, since the two books were published a century apart and the essay uses that gap to account for the difference between the two answers it reports
options.misconception: reads a difference in dates as the essay's principle, which the constant question rules out

options.text: By author, since the essay gives each writer's circumstances before reading either book, so the comparison is between two lives as much as two texts
options.misconception: makes the writers' lives the basis, when what the essay holds constant is a question asked of both texts alike

options.text: By reputation, since one of the books is much better known than the other and the essay opens by saying how widely each of them is read today
options.misconception: takes popularity as a criterion, which says nothing about how the comparison has been conducted

questions.explanation: The test of a thematic comparison is whether one question survives the whole essay, and here it does: the same question is asked of each novel and each novel is read in order to answer it. What that arrangement buys is a comparison in the strict sense, because a reader can see two treatments of one problem side by side and ask which the second makes more of. A thematic basis is also what makes a comparison across kinds of writing possible at all, since two books about different subjects can still be compared by what they do with a single question. The second option brings in a date and then makes the date do the work of an explanation, but a gap of a century is a fact about printing and not a reason either book gives its answer. The third makes biography the basis, and a comparison organised by a writer's circumstances is a comparison of two lives that happens to read books. The fourth opens with a fact about readership and then leaves the question of reception, and reception is not what a held-constant question produces.
questions.hint: Ask what stays the same while the essay moves from one book to the other.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two principles compared, theme against chronology
questions.learningObjective: compare a thematic comparison with a chronological one
questions.stem: Essay A holds one question constant across four novels from four countries and answers it in each. Essay B arranges the same four novels in the order they were written and describes what changes across the four. Which comparison is best supported?

options.text: A is organised by theme and B by chronology, and a thematic comparison can show a shared problem that B's order would place in four separate moments
A is organised by theme and B by chronology, and B is the stronger of the two, since a date is a fact and a theme is only a reader's construction
options.misconception: ranks a checkable fact above a constructed frame, which mistakes ease of verification for value

options.text: Both essays are thematic, since a question put to a novel about its own moment is a theme and the two essays are doing one kind of work
options.misconception: folds chronology into theme, though an order of writing is a different principle from a shared question

options.text: A is organised by form and B by theme, since four books that answer one question must share a kind and the order of writing cannot matter here
options.misconception: swaps the two principles, and books can answer one question without sharing a kind between them

questions.explanation: The two essays are built on different principles and each principle decides what can be seen. A's principle is a question, and holding a question across four books from four countries makes a comparison visible that chronology would dissolve: the same problem being answered in four places, which is the only way to tell whether a problem is a period's problem or a reader's. B's principle is an order, and an order is excellent at showing development, a habit appearing, a device arriving, and unable to show a shared problem unless the books are close enough in date for their adjacency to mean something. Neither principle is the true one, and the choice is a choice about the question. The second option ranks a date above a question because a date is easier to check, which confuses the ease of verifying a piece of scaffolding with the value of what it holds up. The third makes chronology a form of theming, and the two are genuinely different in what they can find. The fourth swaps them and then reasons that books answering one question must be alike in kind, which is a further confusion, since the four novels in question are from four countries and plainly not alike.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two arrangements would break up a shared problem.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a chronological comparison assumes
questions.learningObjective: identify what a chronological arrangement of texts takes for granted
questions.stem: An essay arranges six novels in the order they were written and argues that the earliest of them is the one the other five are replies to. What is the essay's basis, and what is it assuming?

options.text: Chronology, and it is assuming that a later book is a reply to an earlier one, which is a claim about what an author intended and not a consequence of dates
Influence, and it is assuming only that the six books were in circulation for the same readers, which the order of their publication is evidence of
options.misconception: names influence while supplying only availability, and a reply is more than an opportunity to reply

options.text: Form, and it is assuming that a shared shape passes from one book to another, which an arrangement by date is a natural way to suggest
options.misconception: takes a shared shape as given, though nothing about publication order establishes a borrowing of form

options.text: Reception, and it is assuming that readers met the books in the order they appeared, which is what an essay arranged by date describes
options.misconception: describes the arrangement rather than the basis, and reading order is not what the essay is using

questions.explanation: Putting six books in the order they were written is a chronological arrangement, and the argument built on it goes further than the arrangement licenses. The claim that five books are replies to the first is a claim about intention, since a reply is something an author intended and a reader recognised, and an order of dates can establish only that the second book was available when the third was written. Everything else in the claim, that the first shaped the others, that the others took something from it, is additional and needs additional evidence. The second option names the right relation and supplies the wrong support, because circulation is a matter of availability and a book can be available to everyone and used by nobody. The third brings in a borrowing of form and treats the chronology as evidence for it, when a shared shape between two books may be a convention both writers found available. The fourth describes the essay's arrangement and calls it its basis, and then names an assumption about reading order that nothing in the argument requires.
questions.hint: Ask what the order of publication can establish and what it cannot.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Four novels restored to a chain of replies
questions.learningObjective: restore a chronological order in which each text replies to the one before it
questions.stem: Four invented novels have been printed in the wrong order. Restore them so that each is placed after the one it could be read as answering.

options.text: and its second edition answered the first with the same plot and a different ending, which the review called an admission
and it was written because its author had read what the earlier novel's author had read, which is why both books end at a customs house
and its plot was lifted from a serial that had appeared the year before, though the author maintained he had never seen it
and it takes the customs house from the novel before it and makes the building a station, so that the last page is a departure

questions.explanation: Each of the four describes a relation to a text, and only one order lets every relation find its object. The novel lifted from a serial is first, because a borrowing is a reply and it replies to something outside the four, so it cannot be placed after a work it is supposed to have taken from. The second edition is second, since it is by definition a reply to the first and to nothing later, and the review's remark about an admission is a reader's account of that reply being recognised. The novel written from the same reading is third: it is not a second edition of anything, and what it shares with the first is a source rather than a text, which is a weaker relation and one that can only be traced once both texts are in place. The novel that takes the customs house and turns the building into a station is last, because it names the novel before it and builds on the detail it found there, and a book that uses a specific image from another book is on firmer chronological ground than one that shares a source with it. The order as printed puts the borrowing second, so that it appears to answer a book which had not yet existed to be answered.
questions.hint: Find the book that replies to something outside the set, since it cannot come after its reply.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A comparison held inside one form
questions.learningObjective: identify a comparison organised by form
questions.stem: An essay compares a long novel written in many voices with a long poem written in many voices, and finds that the poem marks each change of voice on the page while the novel marks nothing at all. What is the essay's basis of comparison?

options.text: Form, since both texts are being read as instances of one arrangement, that of many voices in a single work, and the differences are differences inside that form
Genre, since a poem and a novel cannot fairly be compared at all and the essay is showing a reader why the two traditions must be kept apart
options.misconception: treats a comparison across kinds as impossible, which is the comparison the essay is conducting

options.text: Theme, since the changes of voice in both works turn on the same question about who may speak for whom, and the essay is tracking that question
options.misconception: supposes a shared question that the essay never states, since the differences given are differences of marking

options.text: Period, since the poem was written a century before the novel and the essay is arguing that marking a change of voice was invented in between
options.misconception: brings in a date the essay has not used, since the comparison is being made inside a single form

questions.explanation: The form is the arrangement the two texts share, and the essay's findings are about how each of them handles it. Many voices in one work is a structural decision, and a text can solve that decision in more than one way: by printing a break so the reader is told, or by running the change into the sentence and trusting the reader to hear it. Because the two texts are being read as instances of one problem, the difference is informative rather than merely different, since a reader learns that the problem admits a marked solution and an unmarked one. The second option rules out the comparison the essay is conducting, and it does so by treating kinds of writing as sealed, which is what a cross-kind comparison exists to test. The third supplies a shared question that the essay never states, and the differences described are not about what the voices argue but about how a change of voice is signalled. The fourth introduces a date and then an invention story, and nothing in the essay's method requires that the later text learned from the earlier one.
questions.hint: Ask what the two texts have in common that makes the difference between them informative.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two readings of the same pair of texts
questions.learningObjective: compare two essays that read the same features at different depths
questions.stem: Essay A compares two texts by the arrangement of their voices and finds that one marks its changes and the other does not. Essay B compares the same two texts by whether each believes a single account can be true and reaches the opposite verdict about the first text. Which comparison is best supported?

options.text: The two are reading one feature at two depths, so the first settles how the text works and the second settles what the working is for, and neither displaces the other
Essay B's comparison is better, because a question about truth can be settled from a text whereas an arrangement of voices can only be described
options.misconception: asserts a hierarchy of questions, and a description is not thereby a weaker kind of reading

options.text: The two findings contradict each other, because a text that marks its changes clearly is a text that doubts its own single account
options.misconception: manufactures a contradiction out of two findings about different features of one text

options.text: Essay A's comparison is better, because arrangement is a feature of a text and belief is a feature of a character, which no comparison can reach
options.misconception: excludes belief from a text on the ground that it belongs to a character, which is where a text most plainly puts it

questions.explanation: The two essays are not competing over a single question, which is why their findings can both stand. What a text does with its voices and what a text believes about a single account are related but not identical, and a text can mark its changes scrupulously because it is confident of each voice and can still be a book that doubts any one of them. Reading the arrangement tells a reader how to read; reading the belief tells a reader what the reading adds up to. The first is the ground of the second and neither is a substitute for it. The second option ranks a question about truth above a question about arrangement on the grounds that one can be settled from the text, when both are read from the text and the arrangement is as checkable as any belief about what a book thinks. The third invents a contradiction, since nothing about marking a change of voice commits a text to believing a single account. The fourth excludes belief from a text altogether, and belief is precisely what a novel puts in the place a person would occupy.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two essays are asking the same question of the two texts.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A likeness drawn from two last pages
questions.learningObjective: explain why a similarity between two endings is superficial
questions.stem: An essay says two invented novels are alike because both end in a railway station, and the essay's whole evidence is the last page of each book. What is wrong with the similarity?

options.text: It has been drawn from the endings rather than from the books, so two final pages can be alike while the works containing them are opposites throughout
It has been drawn from the settings, and a setting is the least reliable evidence a comparison can use because an author may choose a railway for any purpose whatever
options.misconception: makes settings illegitimate as evidence, where a shared setting can be a real point of contact

options.text: It rests on too few examples, since a likeness established by two cases cannot be trusted until a third case is found that shares it
options.misconception: complains about the number of examples when the fault lies in which part of each work was compared

options.text: It depends on the particular editions, since a novel's last page can be set differently in a reprint and may not be the page the writer wrote last
options.misconception: invents a difficulty about printing that the comparison does not depend on

questions.explanation: A comparison is superficial when the feature it names belongs to a part of the work rather than to the work's organising decisions, because a last page is a small part and can be arrived at by any of a great many routes. Two novels can end in a station because one is about departure and the other because the last available train leaves from there, and the reader who has the two final pages in front of them has been given a coincidence without being given anything to compare. The second option is a defensible worry in the abstract and the wrong diagnosis here, since a shared setting can be the most substantial point of contact two books have, and what matters is whether it is the thing the books are built to be about. The third counts cases, and three would not help, because a third book ending in a station would make the pattern more common without making the first two books any more alike in what they are doing. The fourth is a difficulty about printing, and a novel's final page is the final page in any edition.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two examples are a part of the works or the works themselves.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A shared feature read two ways
questions.learningObjective: analyse a likeness that is real and whose significance differs
questions.stem: Essay A says two novels are alike because both contain a chapter in which nothing happens. In the first, the empty chapter is a boy describing one afternoon. In the second, it is a chapter missing from a damaged copy and marked by a gap in the numbering. Which comparison is best supported?

options.text: The likeness is real and the use differs, since one of the two chapters writes quiet and the other records a loss, so the same absence does the same work in neither
There is no likeness at all, since a chapter in which nothing happens cannot be compared with a chapter that is missing, and only one of them is a chapter
options.misconception: dismisses the shared feature on a technicality, though an absence of event is describable in both books

options.text: The likeness is only of length, and a comparison of length is the weakest available, since any two chapters can be made to run to the same number of pages
options.misconception: reduces the comparison to a measurement when what is compared is what the two chapters are for

options.text: The second chapter is the better term of the comparison, since a reader can tell that a chapter is missing whereas a reader cannot tell that nothing has happened
options.misconception: ranks the two by how visible the feature is, which is a claim about evidence and not about likeness

questions.explanation: The two chapters share a feature that can be stated exactly, and a reader is entitled to call them alike on that ground: in both, the sequence of events is interrupted. What they do not share is what the interruption is for, and that is where the comparison earns its keep. A boy describing an afternoon is a chapter that writes quiet, and the quiet is the subject, so that the reader experiences the same flatness the boy does. A gap in a numbering is a different thing entirely, produced by damage, and what the reader experiences is the loss of something that was there, which is a fact about the world of the book rather than about its pace. The second option refuses the likeness on a technicality that does not hold, since a reader reads a missing chapter and an empty chapter with the same attention to the break. The third reduces the comparison to length. The fourth is the interesting error, since the second chapter is indeed the more visible, and visibility is evidence rather than importance.
questions.hint: Ask what the two interruptions are each doing inside their books.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A difference measured by what a text does with a fact
questions.learningObjective: identify a substantive difference between two texts
questions.stem: An essay says two invented novels differ substantially, because in the first a narrator's account of a fire is contradicted by a document and in the second it is contradicted by another character. What makes that difference substantive?

options.text: The difference is in what each book does with being contradicted, so the comparison is of the two treatments of a check and not of the check, which both books supply
The difference is in the presence of a document, since one text offers an outside check and the other offers only another opinion, and an opinion is worth less
options.misconception: counts the strength of the check rather than what each text does with the check it has been given

options.text: The difference is in the space the contradicted account occupies, since in one case it fills a paragraph and in the other it fills a whole chapter of the book
options.misconception: measures the extent of the narration, which is not what the comparison is being made about

options.text: The difference is in the reader's sympathy, since a reader who believes the first narrator is standing in a different position from one who believes the second
options.misconception: places the difference in a reader's response when the two arrangements are in the texts themselves

questions.explanation: Both novels do the same structural thing, which is put a narrator's account where something in the book can check it, and that shared decision is what makes a comparison of their treatments possible at all. A difference is substantive when it is about the work the text makes that check do, and the possibilities are various: the document may be shown to be wrong, in which case the check was theatre; the document may be right, in which case the narrator was deceived; or the book may refuse to say, in which case the checking itself is the subject. A character's contradiction behaves differently again, because a character is inside the fiction and can be wrong for reasons the book will supply. The second option ranks the two kinds of check by strength, which would make the essay a comparison of evidential weight and would explain nothing about the two books. The third measures a narration's length. The fourth locates the difference in the reader, where the two arrangements are not.
questions.hint: Ask what each book makes its check do once the check has happened.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A difference offered in page layout
questions.learningObjective: explain why a formal difference in arrangement is not by itself substantive
questions.stem: An essay claims two invented poems differ substantially because one is printed in four sections and the other in three, and it offers no other observation about either poem. What is wrong with the claim?

options.text: The difference offered is a fact about how the pages are divided rather than about the poems, so a reader has been given an arrangement and not a finding about either text
The difference offered is a genuine formal difference, and an essay is entitled to call a formal difference substantive when the sections carry the argument of the poem
options.misconception: defends the observation, when a claim of substance still has to be supported by evidence about the poems themselves

options.text: The difference offered is too slight to be a difference, since any two printed things may be counted and counting is not a way of reading either poem
options.misconception: insists that counting can never be reading, whereas a formal observation may be the beginning of a reading

options.text: The difference offered concerns form where the essay promised a comparison of theme, and a comparison that changes its basis without announcing it has failed a reader
options.misconception: identifies a change of basis rather than the fault, and no thematic basis was promised here

questions.explanation: A claim that two works differ substantially is a claim about the works, and a fact about the number of sections is a fact about how a work has been laid out on paper. That is not nothing: a section division is a decision about where a reader is to expect a turn, and a poem in three and a poem in four may genuinely place that turn differently. But the essay has offered the count and stopped, so it has asserted a difference and withheld every observation that would make the difference mean anything to a reader. The second option is the strongest defence available and it grants the observation its due while ignoring that a claim of substance is a claim about significance, which requires a reader to be shown what the significance is. The third rules out counting altogether, which is too simple, since a formal observation is often where a reading begins. The fourth identifies a different fault, since the essay never announced a thematic basis, and a change of basis can only be a fault where one was declared.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader has been shown about the poems beyond how they are set.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What would establish a claim of borrowing
questions.learningObjective: state the evidence a claim of influence requires
questions.stem: An essay says a novelist's third novel borrows its structure from an older novel, and its evidence is that both end with the same image of a garden wall seen from a train. What would establish the claim?

options.text: Evidence that the novelist could have read the older novel, and evidence of a pattern rather than of one shared image, since a single coincidence carries no borrowing at all
A statement from the novelist's biographer, since a biographer's account of what an author read is a document rather than another reading of two texts
options.misconception: substitutes testimony about reading for a pattern in the texts, which is the thing the claim is about

options.text: A comparison of the two novels' dates, since a later book cannot borrow from an earlier one unless the dates put them in that order at all
options.misconception: supplies only the trivial half of what is needed, since every influence claim begins with the later text being later

options.text: A third novel that borrows the same image, since a device used more than once is a pattern rather than a coincidence of a single pair
options.misconception: counts instances of a device, where what matters is the shape of the borrowing rather than how often a device recurs

questions.explanation: A claim of borrowing has two halves and the essay has offered neither. The first is access: a novel cannot take from a book its author had no way of reading, and the wall from the train is a coincidence until availability is established. The second is pattern: one shared image is a small thing, and small things arrive independently, whereas a claim about structure is a claim about how a work is put together and has to be shown at that level, over enough of the work to exclude chance. The second option is a document and it is worth having, but a biographer's account of what an author read is testimony about access, and it settles the first half while leaving the pattern to be found in the texts. The third gives the one thing an influence claim never needs help with, since later texts come after earlier ones as a matter of the calendar. The fourth counts the wrong thing: what a third novel borrowed shows that an image was used twice, not that either of the first two books took its structure from anything.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would need to know before the shared image means anything.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Evidential steps of an influence argument
questions.learningObjective: order the steps by which an influence claim is established
questions.stem: Four steps from an invented essay arguing that one novel borrowed its structure from another have been printed out of order. Restore them so that each step is available only after the one before it.

options.text: and only then can the pattern be called a borrowing rather than a coincidence of subject
and the earlier novel was out of print for thirty years and was in the county library from the year before the later one was finished
and the later novel reproduces four episodes of the earlier one and rearranges three of them, which are the four the earlier novel is built from
and the author had borrowed two books that year, and the catalogue still records which two

questions.explanation: The four steps form a dependency, and each of them needs a fact the one before it supplies. The availability comes first because the year it establishes is the year the later steps refer to: the earlier novel being in the county library from a stated year is what makes a borrowing in that year possible at all, and nothing later in the chain can be said without it. The catalogue entry comes second because the step's phrase that year points back to the year the first step has just given, and a signed and dated record of a named borrowing establishes access to a specific book rather than access in general. The pattern comes third, because a decision about coincidence cannot be made before the reader has been shown how much is shared and how it is arranged. The conclusion comes last, since calling the pattern a borrowing is a judgment about the pattern and not about access, and it is a judgment the essay has not been entitled to make until the third step has been read. The order as printed begins with the conclusion, so that the argument appears to end before it has begun.
questions.hint: Find the step that supplies the year the other two refer to.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A source against an influence
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a claim of influence from a claim of a source
questions.stem: An essay says a poet's earliest work shows the influence of the psalms, on the ground that the psalms were available to be read. How does that claim differ from the claim that the psalms were a source for the work?

options.text: Availability is a fact about what could have been read and influence is a claim about what the poet did with what was read, so the second needs evidence of a use and not merely of an opportunity
There is no difference between them, since a book available to a poet is a book that shaped the poet, and shaping is simply availability over a period of time
options.misconception: identifies availability with influence, which is the confusion the item exists to catch

options.text: A source is what a work was written out of and an influence is what a work resembles, so the first concerns composition and the second concerns likeness
options.misconception: assigns the two words to different objects, though both name a relation between two texts

options.text: A source is earlier and an influence is later, so the two words differ only in which of the two texts is being named and the claim is the same one
options.misconception: makes the distinction a matter of grammatical position, so the two claims come to the same thing

questions.explanation: The two claims are about different relations, and the difference is the whole content of the item. That the psalms were available is a fact about the world in which the poet worked, and it removes one possible objection, namely that the poet could not have read them. It says nothing about what the poet did, and a poet can have the psalms open on a desk for a decade and write nothing of them. A claim of influence requires a use, which means something in the poem that a reader can point to and connect to something in the psalms, and a claim of source is stronger still, since it asserts that the work was made out of the other rather than that it shows its marks. The second option is the error that makes weak influence claims common, and it is worth noticing that it treats influence as a background condition when it is a relation between two texts. The third assigns the words to different objects when both are relations, and the fourth reduces the difference to which text is the subject of the sentence, which leaves the argument untouched.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would have to see in the poem itself.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Evidence graded by the claim it can carry
questions.learningObjective: order four kinds of evidence by the strength of the claim each supports
questions.stem: Four kinds of evidence used in an invented essay arguing that one text influenced another have been printed in the order the essay used them. Reorder them from the weakest to the strongest claim they can carry.

options.text: the later text reproduces four episodes of the earlier one and rearranges three of them, which are the four the earlier text is built from
the later text shares a rare device with the earlier one, and no other writer of the century is recorded as using it
the later text is dated after the earlier one, so nothing about the order of the two excludes a borrowing between them
the later text's author is recorded as having borrowed the earlier one, and the catalogue entry is signed and dated

questions.explanation: The four kinds of evidence differ in what they can be made to carry, and the ordering follows from the claim each one reaches. The dates come last in strength because they carry the least: all they establish is that the borrowing was possible, which is a claim about the calendar and rules nothing out. A rare device comes next, since rarity raises the probability of a link without establishing one, and a device can travel by convention, by coincidence, or by borrowing, and a single instance cannot say which. A pattern in the structure is stronger again, because four episodes taken and three rearranged is a claim about how a work is put together rather than about a feature of it, and chance does not rearrange four episodes that are the four a book is built from. The catalogue entry is the strongest, because it is a document that names the act, signed and dated, and it does not have to be inferred from the texts at all. The order as printed begins with the pattern, which is a way of making the argument look stronger than its evidence.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four could be true of two books that had nothing to do with each other.

questions.topic: Genre and period before a question can be asked
questions.learningObjective: state what must be established before a formal anomaly is significant
questions.stem: An essay asks why a poem published in 1798 prints a footnote explaining a classical allusion. What does the essay have to establish before the question is worth asking?

options.text: Whether the poem's genre and moment would normally expect the allusion to be explained, since without that expectation the footnote is neither surprising nor significant at all
Whether the poet was a scholar, since a writer's learning is the simplest explanation of a classical allusion in a poem of any date whatever and needs no further account
options.misconception: jumps to a biographical cause before establishing what makes the feature remarkable in the first place

options.text: Whether other poems of the same decade carry footnotes, since a single example cannot show that the practice belongs to the period rather than to one poet alone
options.misconception: demands a survey where the item requires a comparison of expectations, which is a smaller thing than a survey

options.text: Whether the footnote was in the first edition, since a note added by a later editor is a different document from one that a reader of 1798 would have seen
options.misconception: assumes the footnote is a later addition, which the question about genre and moment does not require

questions.explanation: A feature only means something relative to what was expected, and the expectation is supplied by two things at once: the kind of text and the moment. A footnote is a way of writing to a reader, and whether it is expected depends on what kind of reader a poem of that kind in that decade is presumed to have. If glossing a classical reference were ordinary, the footnote would be routine and there would be nothing to explain; if it were unheard of, the footnote becomes evidence about who the poet thought was reading. Either way the question cannot be asked until the expectation has been stated. The second option supplies a cause before the anomaly has been established, and a scholar's learning is a perfectly good explanation of an allusion and no explanation at all of a gloss. The third asks for a survey, which is a larger undertaking than the item requires, since the comparison that matters is between this poem and what poems of its kind were doing. The fourth raises a real question about editions while assuming the answer, and a footnote present in the first edition would be a very different fact from one added later.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader of a poem of that kind in that decade would have expected.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two expectations, two forms, two conclusions
questions.learningObjective: compare a comparison made across genres and periods
questions.stem: Essay A compares a poem of 1798, which prints a footnote glossing a classical allusion, with a novel of 1902, which prints an unglossed line of Latin. The essay concludes that the poem is writing for a reader who needs help and the novel is not. Which comparison is best supported?

options.text: It is supported once each text is read against what its own form and moment expects, since a glossed allusion in a poem and an unglossed one in a novel are not like appearances
It is supported by the dates alone, since 1798 is early enough for readers to need help with a classical reference and 1902 is late enough for them not to need it
options.misconception: makes chronology decide a question that is about the relation between a form and what its readers expect

options.text: It is not supported, because a poem and a novel are different forms and no comparison between their readers can be made across a difference so wide
options.misconception: declares the cross-genre comparison impossible, which is the comparison the essay is conducting

options.text: It is supported by the difference in the Latin, since one text glosses the phrase and the other does not, and glossing is what marks a reader in need of help
options.misconception: confuses a linguistic choice with a claim about readers, which need not travel together

questions.explanation: The conclusion is defensible, and what makes it defensible is that the essay has compared two situations rather than two dates. A classical allusion in a poem and an unglossed line of Latin in a novel are not the same act, because the forms make different assumptions about who is reading and about how much a reader is expected to bring. A printed footnote in a poem is a writer deciding that the page should carry the explanation; an unglossed quotation in a novel is a writer deciding that a character should speak as a character would. Both are claims about readers, and they are claims made inside forms, which is why the comparison has to be read against each form's own expectation. The second option hands the work to the dates, and dates are silent about forms; a reader in 1798 reading a novel would have met the same unglossed Latin and been expected to manage it. The third rules out the comparison the essay is making, which is the mistake that a cross-form comparison exists to avoid. The fourth turns a claim about reading into a claim about vocabulary, and the two can come apart, since a text may gloss a word and still be writing for an expert.
questions.hint: Ask what each form expects of its reader before asking what each text does.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What two translations of one word disclose
questions.learningObjective: explain what a difference between two translations reveals
questions.stem: One poem exists in two translations. The first renders its central word with a common noun, and the second with a compound invented to hold two meanings at once. What does the difference between the two renderings let a reader compare?

options.text: The two translators' accounts of what the word is doing in the original, since inventing a compound is a decision about the original's sense and not about the target language alone
Which of the two translators is the more accurate, since a coinage departs from the original where a common noun reproduces what the original plainly said
options.misconception: sets the two renderings against a standard of accuracy, when the difference is evidence about a reading rather than a verdict on one

options.text: How difficult the original language is, since a word that resists an ordinary English equivalent is evidence about the language and not about a reading of it
options.misconception: redirects the comparison to the source language, which is not what two renderings of one word actually disclose

options.text: Which audience each version was made for, since a common noun reaches a general reader and a compound reaches a specialist, so the choice is really a commercial one
options.misconception: reduces a reading to a marketing decision, which is one possible motive and not what the choice shows

questions.explanation: A translator who uses a common noun is committing to one sense and accepting that the other is lost, and a translator who coins a compound is refusing that loss and paying for it in a phrase no speaker would use. That difference is a difference about the original, not about English: one translator thinks the word means a thing and the other thinks it holds a pun that English cannot carry in a single word, and the only way to learn which is right is to argue about the poem. The second option converts the comparison into a competition, which throws away the evidence the pair provides, since a coinage can be scrupulous or desperate. The third points the comparison at the source language, and although difficulty is real, two renderings disclose what two readers think a word is doing rather than what a language permits. The fourth is the commercial explanation, and it is a possible motive, but a decision about which readers to reach would not usually require a compound, and it does not tell a reader anything about the poem.
questions.hint: Ask what each translator had to believe about the original to write what they wrote.

questions.learningObjective: compare two translated titles and what their difference discloses
questions.stem: A novel's title is rendered in one translation by a phrase naming its subject matter, and in another by a phrase naming a mood. What has the pair of renderings made comparable?

The relative accuracy of the two titles, since a phrase naming a subject is closer to what a title does and a phrase naming a mood is a liberty the translator has taken
options.misconception: assumes one convention of titling is correct and measures both renderings against it

options.text: The two languages' conventions about titling, since a language that prefers naming subjects and a language that prefers naming moods will differ in exactly this manner
options.misconception: attributes a difference to a whole convention, which two translated titles cannot establish

options.text: The contents of the book, since a title is a promise about a work and two different promises cannot both be kept by one book at the same time
options.misconception: infers a difference in the book's contents from a difference in its titles, which is not what a translation shows

questions.explanation: Titles are the one place in a book where a translator has to make a decision in a language rather than about a language, and the decision is what the pair exposes. That is a fact about how translators read, and it is available to any reader who knows two versions. The second option sets up a standard and measures against it, and the standard is assumed rather than argued, since a title that names a mood is doing something titles do. The third makes two titles into evidence about a whole language, which would need many examples and would still not tell a reader what this book is centrally about. The fourth draws a conclusion about the book itself, and two renderings of one title are two readings of a promise, not two pieces of evidence about the keeping of it.
questions.hint: Ask what sentence about the book each title is making.

questions.topic: Two adaptations holding one element constant
questions.learningObjective: explain what a pair of adaptations that vary one element reveals
questions.stem: Two stage adaptations of one play are compared. The first keeps the play's language and changes the staging. The second keeps the staging and rewrites the language. What does the pair let a reader examine?

options.text: Which of the two things a production can change without loss, since holding one constant while altering the other shows where the work's weight is not resting
Which of the two adaptations is the more faithful, since a version that keeps the words stands closer to the original than one that keeps the pictures
options.misconception: assumes fidelity is measured by one element, which is exactly the doubt the pair is designed to raise

options.text: How a play of this period was usually staged, since two versions together give a reader a range within which a period's practice can be located
options.misconception: reads a comparison of two instances as a survey of a period's practice, which two versions cannot supply

options.text: Whether the play can be produced at all in a modern building, since one of the two versions' changes is what a modern stage would require of it
options.misconception: asks a question about buildings that neither version's difference of kind is able to answer

questions.explanation: A production has two kinds of material, the words and the arrangements, and the pair is built to vary one at a time. A version that keeps every line and reworks the staging is showing a reader what the play's language can survive without its pictures, and a version that keeps the staging and rewrites the language is showing what the staging can carry without the lines. Where a change produces no visible loss, the weight of the work is not resting there, and that is a real finding about a play rather than a comment on taste. The second option puts the two versions on a scale of fidelity and so assumes the answer, since a play is not a document and the element a modern audience loses first is not automatically the element that carries it. The third makes two instances into a survey, and a range drawn from two versions is the widest range two versions can give. The fourth is a question about buildings, and neither version's difference of kind is a fact about a stage's dimensions.
questions.hint: Ask which element each version had to do without, and what still worked.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Four versions ranked by distance from a source
questions.learningObjective: order adaptations by how much of the original survives in them
questions.stem: Four invented versions of one stage play have been printed in the wrong order. Restore them from the version that has changed least to the version that has changed most.

options.text: and the same script was performed for forty years with the same costumes, and the only thing that ever changed was the lighting
and the songs were kept word for word and the set was rebuilt in its original shape, but the plot was rearranged to end somewhere else
and the dialogue was rewritten for a smaller stage and the songs were cut, though the plot was left exactly as it was
and the music was rewritten and the ending moved and the dialogue cut down to the four lines the cast could remember

questions.explanation: The versions differ in how much of the play is left, and the order follows from counting what each one still has of the play's three kinds of material: the words, the music, and the arrangements. The version performed for forty years with the same costumes has altered one element, since only the lighting was ever touched, and a repertory able to absorb a change for four decades is a repertory that did not need the play altered at all. The version that keeps the songs word for word and rebuilds the set in its original shape comes next: the play's music and its look are intact and only its structure has been moved, so a reader can still find the whole work inside it. The version that rewrites the dialogue and cuts the songs comes after that, and it is further from the original even though it keeps the plot, because a stage play's words are its text and a text that has been rewritten is no longer the text. The last version has altered all three kinds at once, and the four lines the cast could remember are the point at which nothing survives but the outline. The order as printed began with a version that had already rewritten the dialogue and cut the songs.
questions.hint: Ask which of the words, the music, and the arrangements each version still has.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What makes two narrators comparable
questions.learningObjective: state what must be established before two narrators can be compared
questions.stem: An essay compares the narrator of an invented nineteenth-century novel with the narrator of a modern one, and argues that both are unreliable, since in each the account is contradicted by a document. What must the essay establish before that comparison holds?

options.text: That unreliability is the same property in both, which means showing how each narrator stands in relation to the events rather than what each is like as a person
That the two books come from a single period, since a narrator's reliability is a convention of a moment and cannot be compared across a century and a half
options.misconception: makes reliability a convention of a period, when the question is each narrator's relation to events

options.text: That both texts employ the same device, since a narrator contradicted by a document is one technique and comparing techniques is not comparing narrators
options.misconception: insists on one shared device, which would make the essay a comparison of techniques rather than of narrators

options.text: That one narrator is less unreliable than the other, since a comparison of two narrators has to end in a difference of degree and not in a likeness
options.misconception: requires a verdict of degree, though two narrators are comparable without either being worse

questions.explanation: The essay has found the same feature in two books, and what it must now show is that the feature means the same thing in each, since a comparison of two things is only possible when the thing being compared is a thing rather than two things under one name. Unreliability is a relation between a narrator and what happens, and a narrator contradicted by a document in an 1840 novel and one contradicted by a document in a modern novel are related in that relation, even though everything else about them differs. The second option makes reliability a matter of period, which would rule out most of literary comparison and does not address the essay's actual difficulty. The third insists on a single shared technique, and a technique is not a narrator; two books can use the same device for different purposes and produce two different questions about their tellers. The fourth demands a verdict of degree, which is a conclusion rather than a precondition, and a comparison can establish that two narrators are comparably unreliable without saying which is worse.
questions.hint: Ask what the word unreliable is doing in each of the two books.

questions.topic: A comparison that confuses a narrator with a period
questions.learningObjective: identify what an essay compared when it claimed to compare narrators
questions.stem: An essay argues that the narrator of one invented novel cannot be trusted because he is a man of his period, and that the narrator of a second can be trusted because he is not. What has this essay actually compared?

options.text: The two narrators' periods rather than their reliability, since a narrator's era tells a reader nothing about how his account stands against what happened in it
The two narrators' reliability, and it has done so correctly, since a narrator shaped by his century will see only what that century was able to see
options.misconception: defends a period-based test of accuracy, which the essay's own pairing of the two cases shows does not work

options.text: The two narrators' trustworthiness as persons, since the essay treats a man's character as settling the question of whether his account is accurate
options.misconception: settles accuracy by character, which is a different question from whether an account can be checked

options.text: Nothing in particular, since both claims are about narrators and any comparison of two narrators is a comparison of their reliability
options.misconception: assumes any two claims about narrators are on one axis, which is the error the pair was written to expose

questions.explanation: The essay's test is a fact about a narrator's date and not a fact about his account, and the pairing shows it, because the essay accepts one narrator and rejects another on the same criterion without ever saying what the criterion is doing. A narrator shaped by his century is a fact, and what such a narrator can see is a fair question, but a reader who cannot be shown that his account is contradicted will be believed whatever century made him, and the essay has offered no contradiction for either man. The third substitutes character for accuracy, which are two different questions, and a likable narrator can be wrong in every particular while an unpleasant one is exactly right. The fourth assumes that any two claims about narrators are on a single axis, and the whole difficulty lies in finding out whether they are.
questions.hint: Ask what evidence about either account the essay has supplied.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: One image, two traditions
questions.learningObjective: explain what a claim about a shared motif across traditions must establish
questions.stem: An essay finds the same image, a door left open, at the centre of a poem from one tradition and a play from another, and concludes that the two are the same motif. What has the essay not established?

options.text: That the image does the same work in each, since a motif is a set of associations a tradition builds around a thing and a shared image need not carry a shared set at all
That the two works are of comparable seriousness, since a motif is a device of serious writing and cannot attach to a poem and a play in the same breath
options.misconception: makes a judgement about seriousness where a claim about associations is what has to be checked

options.text: That the two traditions have ever been in contact, since a motif can only travel from one to another where there has been some meeting between the two peoples
options.misconception: requires contact between traditions, which would prevent most comparisons of works that never met

options.text: That the image is old in both, since a motif's force depends on how long a tradition has carried it and a recent invention cannot be one in either place
options.misconception: ties a motif's force to age, though an image can be traditional in a culture without being old in it

questions.explanation: A motif is not a thing but a thing plus a history of use, and the history is what does the work. A door left open in one tradition may carry every story in which someone left and did not come back, while in another the same image may be a fact about a house, and a reader who knows the first set and not the second will recognise the image and miss the point. Since what the essay has is an identical image in two places, the missing half is exactly the question of what each tradition has made of it, and without that the resemblance is a resemblance of vocabulary. The second option is a judgement about the standing of the works, which has no bearing on what the image does in either. The third requires contact, and it would rule out comparing any two traditions that never met, which is most of what comparative reading is for. The fourth ties a motif to age, which is a plausible and common confusion with a tradition, and an image can be traditional in a culture without being old in it.
questions.hint: Ask what each tradition has already made of the image before it is used.

questions.topic: A shared image working in opposite directions
questions.learningObjective: analyse a comparison of two images that misses how each works
questions.stem: A poem closes with an open door that nobody crosses, and a play ends with a door left open on the stage while a family talks behind it. The essay claims both images stand for a future the characters cannot reach. What has the essay not accounted for?

options.text: That the poem's door is shut off by the ending while the play's stays available to an audience, so the two images work in opposite directions on hope
That the play's door is a piece of scenery, since a stage door left open is a practical necessity of the stage rather than an image of anything at all
options.misconception: reduces a stage image to scenery, which is a claim about props and not about what the image does to a reader

options.text: That a poem's image and a play's image belong to different kinds of work, so no comparison of them can be made without a rule the essay has not given
options.misconception: insists on a kind of difference that would make any comparison of a poem and a play impossible

options.text: Neither image is traditional enough to compare, so the essay should have chosen two examples that are properly motifs rather than closing images of a door
options.misconception: attacks the choice of examples instead of the claim, which can be tested with the examples given

In the poem the door is the last thing a reader sees and the door's door is the one nobody will cross, so the image is closed off by the very ending that displays it, and what a reader is left with is a future described as unavailable. The third rules out the cross-kind comparison the essay is conducting, which is the whole point of making it. The fourth turns on the choice of examples rather than the claim, and the claim can be tested with the examples actually given.
questions.hint: Ask what each work is still able to do with its door after the final line.

questions.topic: The same word for two different emblems
questions.learningObjective: explain why two culturally different emblems are not the same symbol
questions.stem: An essay compares a white lily in one European emblem with a white lotus in a South Asian one, and says the two are a single symbol of purity. What has the essay overlooked?

That the two flowers are botanically different plants, so the comparison fails as a claim about nature before it is tested as a claim about meaning

options.text: That purity is an abstract, and an abstract cannot be carried by any flower, so neither of the two emblems is a symbol of anything whatever

options.text: Give up the approach, since comparing figures across traditions requires some shared history between them and no such history has been offered here

questions.learningObjective: identify what is weakest in a claim that a theme is universal
questions.stem: An essay argues that the longing to be recognised is a theme common to all literature, on the ground that it appears in a Greek play, a Japanese novel and an Icelandic saga. What is weakest about the argument?

options.text: That three examples cannot establish a universality, and a theme described as common to everything is a description of people rather than a finding about any text
That the three works are too far apart in date, so no reader could judge whether the longing is a fashion of a period or a permanent condition
options.misconception: makes the spread of dates the fault, when a claim of universality is not rescued by examples close in time

options.text: That two of the three works do not count as literature of the kind the claim is about, so the example set is smaller than it appears to be
options.misconception: excludes two of the three examples on a technicality, which leaves the movement from three cases to all literature untouched

options.misconception: objects to the wording of the theme rather than to the reasoning that generalises from examples

questions.explanation: The inference is from three cases to a whole, and no quantity of well-chosen examples fixes it, because a claim about all literature cannot be established by induction. What the three examples actually establish is that the longing appears in a Greek play, a Japanese novel and an Icelandic saga, and a reader who stopped there would have learned something specific. The trouble begins with the theme's wording: described as common to all literature, a longing to be recognised has stopped being a feature of any work and become a feature of persons, at which point it can be found anywhere because it is everywhere. The second option makes the spread of dates the fault, and dates would not help, since a claim of universality fails the same way whether its examples are close together or centuries apart. The third reduces the example set without touching the reasoning. The fourth objects to the theme's phrasing rather than to the argument, and a different phrasing would produce the same three cases and the same generalisation.
questions.hint: Ask what the three examples establish and what the claim goes on to say.

questions.stem: An essay claims filial duty is a universal theme, because a son stays with his father in a Greek tragedy and a son stays with his mother in a modern novel. Which observation would complicate the claim most?

That one of the works was written in a language the essay's author does not read, so the reading of that son's decision may well be mistaken in that case
options.misconception: raises a question about the essay's competence rather than about the scope of its claim

options.text: That the two sons are of very different ages, so the claim is comparing a young man's duty with an old man's and the two are not like things at all

The second option questions whether the essay has read one of the works, which is a fair worry about any reading and not a complication of the claim itself. The third treats a difference in the situations as a difference in the theme, and the variations are what a theme varies through. The fourth, whatever its merits as a distinction, records a common feature and so supports rather than complicates.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The core claim of a formalist reading
questions.learningObjective: state the core claim of a critical framework
questions.stem: A critic says of a poem, "The poem means what its language does, and a reader who goes on to ask what the poet intended has left the poem behind." What is this framework's core claim?

options.text: That a text is a system of language producing its meanings in use, so interpretation is a matter of describing what the text does rather than what anyone meant by it
That a poem's meaning is fixed once its words are fixed, so a reader's task is to recover a single sense and to reject every other as a failure of attention
options.misconception: makes the claim a claim about stability of meaning, which is a different framework's position

options.text: That a poem means whatever its readers have understood it to mean, so no reading can be wrong and a critic's work is to describe variety rather than to argue
options.misconception: confuses a claim about language with a claim about readers, which the sentence does not make

options.text: That a poem's meaning lies in the history that produced it, so the words are evidence about a moment rather than about a meaning in themselves at all
options.misconception: substitutes a claim about context, which is the position the sentence explicitly turns away from

questions.explanation: The sentence makes a claim about where meaning comes from and about where a reader should stop looking, and both halves belong to the same position. Meaning is produced by language in use, so a text is an object whose workings can be described, and the intention of the person who wrote it is a fact about a person and not about the workings. The turn on the reader who goes on to ask what the poet intended is what makes the position recognisable, since it is not a claim that intentions do not exist but a claim about what would settle a question about the poem. The second option substitutes a claim about stability, and stability is a different matter entirely, since a fixed meaning is not what a theory of language in use produces. The third confuses the claim about language with a claim about readers, and the sentence says nothing about how many readings a poem has had. The fourth puts in the position the critic is rejecting.
questions.hint: Ask what the critic says a reader should stop looking for, and why.

questions.topic: A claim about language beside a claim about moment
questions.learningObjective: compare two critics who describe the same line on different principles
questions.stem: Critic A says of a line in an invented poem, "The word cold does the work of three adjectives, and a reader who looks for a fourth has misunderstood what the poem is doing." Critic B says, "The word cold is doing that work in 1911, and a poem of 1911 that spent four adjectives on the cold would have been saying something else." Which comparison is best supported?

options.text: The two are compatible, since the first describes what the language does and the second describes what a particular language was doing it in
The first critic is right and the second is wrong, since a claim about a moment is a claim about a period and a poem's language cannot be dated into error
options.misconception: sets the two up as rivals and dismisses one by a rule about dating, which is not what either critic said

options.text: The second critic is right and the first wrong, because a word's work cannot be described at all without knowing which language and which century it was used in
options.misconception: uses the second critic's own premise to dismiss the first, though accepting that premise is accepting his position

options.text: Both critics are describing the same act, since a word does in 1911 exactly what it does in every other century and nothing about a word changes between them
options.misconception: denies the premise the second critic relies on, and the pair exists to show it cannot be denied

questions.explanation: The two critics are describing the same line and asking different questions of it, and the difference is not a disagreement until somebody treats the questions as rivals. A asks what the language is doing, and the answer is that a single word is carrying a weight three words would have carried, which is a fact about the poem and can be established by reading it. B asks what that weight is doing in this language at this date, and the answer is that a poem of 1911 that had spent four adjectives on the cold would have been making a different speech, which is a fact about a moment and can be established by comparison with other poems of the moment. Both descriptions are true of the same word, and a reader who accepts both knows more about the line than either gave alone. The second option invents a conflict and then rules one side out by a rule about dating that neither critic invoked. The third uses B's premise against A, and B's premise is a claim that a word's work is historically specific, which is precisely what makes A's description incomplete rather than wrong. The fourth denies the premise outright and so declares the second critic's question unaskable.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two critics are answering the same question or two questions.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a formal reading counts
questions.learningObjective: identify what a formal reading attends to
questions.stem: A formal reading of an invented poem counts its sentences, notes that six of its nine line endings coincide with the ends of clauses, and says nothing whatever about the century. What is the reading attending to?

options.text: The arrangement of the text, since the relation between line endings and clauses is a fact about how the poem is put together and not about anything outside it
The date of the text, since counting a poem's lines is a routine way of placing it in its century and the pattern found would settle the placement
options.misconception: treats a count of lines as dating evidence, which is a claim about history and not about form

options.text: The meaning of the text, since a pattern of line endings is a pattern of sense and the reading is only reporting the sense the pattern produces
options.misconception: confuses arrangement with meaning, where a pattern of endings is a fact about shape before it is a fact about sense

options.text: The effect of the text, since six coincidences in nine is a measurable response and a reader's response is what the pattern exists to produce
options.misconception: calls a measurement of form a measurement of response, which are two different kinds of finding

questions.explanation: Everything the reading offers is internal to the poem, and that is the test of what it is attending to. A count of sentences and a count of the places where a line ends and a clause ends are both measurements of the poem's own arrangement, and the relation between them is a relation inside the text that a reader can check without knowing anything about when the poem was written or what it was meant to produce. That is the discipline a formal reading imposes on itself: describe the text's making before saying anything about its meaning or its effect, because a claim about meaning and a claim about shape are easier to dispute separately. The second option turns a count of lines into dating evidence, which would require a relation between the length of lines and the year of writing that no one has established. The third collapses shape into sense, and a pattern of endings is a fact about the page before it is a fact about what is being said. The fourth converts a measurement into a response, which is a different kind of claim and needs a different kind of evidence.
questions.hint: Ask what the reading would still be able to say if the poem's date were unknown.

questions.topic: A formal reading asked to connect a device to a subject
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a formal reading's answer to a question about subject
questions.stem: A formal reading explains the ending of a poem by the fact that its last line contains the same sound as its first, and a reader asks what that has to do with the poem's subject. Which is the strongest reply the reading can make?

options.text: That the recurrence is a fact of the poem's making, and a reading that cannot connect such a fact to a subject has not yet said what the fact is for
That the reader is asking something the poem does not raise, since a subject is a matter of theme and a sound is a matter of form and the two do not meet
options.misconception: dismisses the question instead of answering it, which is what a reading has to avoid if it is to be taken seriously

options.text: That a subject is not a property a poem has at all, so the request is made in a category the poem does not belong to and cannot be answered inside it
options.misconception: makes a claim about categories that is itself a critical position and does not follow from the reading given

options.text: That the sound is short and the line is long, so what a reader ought to respond to is the pair of measurements rather than anything about the subject
options.misconception: offers a description of two facts, which is not a reason why either of them matters

questions.explanation: A formal reading is restricted, not silent, and the restriction says nothing about what a reading may not be asked. The reply has to concede the restriction and then go on, because a reader's question is a reasonable one and a reading that treats it as a mistake in the reader has lost the only exchange it will ever have with a reader who is not inside its discipline. The sound that returns at the last line is a fact about the making, and the next question is what a maker does with such a fact, which is not a question the formal discipline forbids and in fact depends on. The second option refuses the exchange by declaring the two to be different departments, and a reading that can be used to prove anything is not being used for anything. The third makes a large claim about categories, which is itself a position about what a poem is and not a reply to a reader's question. The fourth describes the two facts again, and repeating a fact is not a reason for it.
questions.hint: Ask what the reading can add once it has made its observation.

questions.topic: Looking for the system beneath a text
questions.learningObjective: state what a structuralist reading seeks
questions.stem: A critic argues that a single invented novel cannot be understood until the system of conventions its readers share has been described, because every element in it means by contrast with what a novel of that kind would have put in that place instead. What is the critic looking for?

options.text: The underlying system that gives a text's elements their meaning, since what any one element means is fixed by its position among the alternatives its form allows
The author's plan for the novel, since the conventions a writer followed are best discovered by asking what the writer meant to use them for in the first place
options.misconception: substitutes a writer's intentions for the system of conventions the sentence describes

options.text: The novel's place among the books that came after it, since a text belongs to a system and the clearest way of fixing a book's system is to date it
options.misconception: makes the system a chronological sequence, where the alternatives named are of one kind rather than of another

options.text: The reader's habit of expectation, since what a reader brings to a text is the system that gives the text its meanings and a critic can measure that habit
options.misconception: locates the system in a reader's mind, though the system described is what the text is built out of

questions.explanation: The critic's method is to refuse the single object and go looking for the relations that make it readable. A convention is a set of possibilities rather than a rule, and an element in a novel means what it means because of the other things that could have stood in its place, which is why the critic's test is a counterfactual about the form. Nothing can be understood until that system is described, because there is nothing to understand it in, and this is the point at which a structuralist reading differs from a close one. The second option puts the writer back at the centre and converts conventions into intentions. The third makes the system a sequence of books, and while texts do belong to groups, the system described here is made of the alternatives a single form allows at a single position. The fourth locates the system in a reader's mind, which is a different framework's territory, and the conventions the critic is describing are properties of the form whether or not any reader holds them.
questions.hint: Ask what the sentence says the meaning of an element depends on.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A convention mistaken for a statement
questions.learningObjective: explain the fault in a reading that takes a form's habit for a claim
questions.stem: A critic argues of an invented novel, "Every chapter ends on a question, and since the form has no other way of closing, the novel's whole argument is that nothing can be settled." What is the objection to that argument?

options.text: It takes a habit of the form for a statement the novel is making, when a device available to any novel of that kind marks only that the writer had it available
It miscounts, since a novel's chapters cannot all end on questions and a critic who says they do has plainly not read to the end of the book
options.misconception: supplies a miscount the argument does not depend on, since the claim is about what the device means

options.text: It describes a feature of the printed page rather than of the story, so the argument is about punctuation and not about the novel's meaning at all
options.misconception: reduces the argument to typography, whereas a chapter's ending is a decision about how a unit of narrative closes

options.text: It jumps too far, since a claim that nothing can be settled has to be argued rather than read off a repeated habit of ending chapters in questions
options.misconception: treats the jump as a matter of emphasis when the gap between a convention and a statement is the fault itself

questions.explanation: The critic's sentence contains the whole argument and both halves of it can be tested. The observation is that the chapters end on questions, and the observation is probably fine. The inference is that the novel is therefore arguing that nothing can be settled, and the inference requires the device to be the novel's own rather than the form's, which is what the critic's own clause gives away by saying the form has no other way of closing. A habit shared by every novel of the kind is available to any writer who wants it and means nothing until a text does something particular with it; a book in which every chapter closes on a question is a book in which a reader has been given an appetite for the unresolved, and an appetite is a structure, not a proposition. The second option invents a miscount that the argument does not need, since the inference would be just as bad with fewer chapters. The third reduces a narrative decision to typography. The fourth treats the fault as one of emphasis, when what is missing is the step from a form's habit to this text's statement.
questions.hint: Ask whether the device belongs to this novel or to novels of its kind.
