questions.topic: What a historical reading restores
questions.learningObjective: state what a historical reading restores to a text
questions.stem: A critic argues that a novel published in 1848 represents a view of the family which a reader of 1848 would have recognised as a position, and that this is what the novel is doing at that moment. What is the critic restoring?

options.text: The situation in which the novel appeared, so a claim about what it was doing becomes a claim about a text arriving at one point among others of its own moment
The author's intention, since a novel of 1848 was written by a person who held the view the critic has found and the critic is recovering that person's belief
options.misconception: confuses a text's historical situation with the mind of the person who wrote it

options.text: The novel's influence, since what a novel does at the moment it appears is the effect it has on the readers who receive it before anyone else does
options.misconception: turns a claim about the moment of production into a claim about reception, which is a different enquiry

options.text: The text's vocabulary, since a novel of 1848 can only use the words available to it and the critic's first business is to establish which words those were
options.misconception: reduces historical reading to a study of vocabulary, though the claim concerns a view of the family

questions.explanation: The critic's claim is about a text in a situation, and the value of a historical reading lies in the fact that a text means different things at different times and that one of those meanings can be recovered. A novel of 1848 appearing among other novels of 1848 is doing something in company, and the critic's job is to say what that company made available, what a reader could recognise in 1848, and what a reader today cannot see at all. What the critic is restoring is a set of conditions rather than a person, and that is the whole difference between a historical claim and a biographical one. The second option puts the author back at the centre, and a writer's belief is a fact about a writer. The third converts production into reception and so answers a different question about the same book. The fourth reduces the whole discipline to word history, and although a novel's vocabulary is a real part of its moment, the claim in front of us is about a view of the family and not about a choice of words.
questions.hint: Ask whether the claim is about a text, a person, or a set of conditions.

questions.topic: A historical explanation offered as the only reading
questions.learningObjective: identify what a historical explanation still has to account for
questions.stem: A critic says that the heroine of an invented novel leaves her husband's house in 1857 because the law of that year gave a wife her own property, and adds that this is the only way to read the ending. What is the objection to that claim?

options.text: That the law establishes what was available and not what a character did, since a reader has to be shown that this woman's circumstances made leaving the choice she could see
That the date of the law has to be established from the novel's own text, since a critic may not bring a document to a book that does not mention one
options.misconception: objects to the sourcing of a date, which is not what the critic's claim turns on

options.text: That a plot's ending is a formal decision about how a narrative closes, and no law outside the text can decide what a character will do in the end
options.misconception: insists that a plot is a formal matter, which would make most historical explanation impossible

options.text: That the novel never mentions property or any law, so the critic has imported the whole of the explanation and the reader cannot be expected to supply it
options.misconception: requires textual mention, and a text's silence about a law is a normal condition and not a bar to explaining it

A wife of 1857 could leave, which is a real and important fact, and it changes the ending from an impropriety into a possibility; but a possibility is not a decision, and a reading that stops there has described the conditions without showing that the woman in this novel saw them the way the critic does. The phrase that this is the only way to read makes the problem worse, because it claims that no motive of any other kind is available to a reader, and nothing in the law forbids a reader from finding one. The second option is a rule about sourcing that would make historical reading impossible, since a text's silence about a law is the normal condition of a novel and not evidence against the law. The third makes plots immune to history. The fourth repeats the second objection as though silence were disproof.
questions.hint: Ask what the law explains and what it leaves for the critic to show.

questions.topic: Meaning as a meeting of text and reader
questions.learningObjective: state the core claim of a reader-response reading
questions.stem: A critic argues that a poem's ending is a collaboration between the text and the reader, and that a reader who is not unsettled by it has read a different poem from the one that was written. What is the claim?

options.text: That meaning is made in the meeting of a text and a reader, so what a text does is bounded by what a reader can do with it and neither account is the whole event alone
That the reader is the author of the poem, so the words are only a starting point and everything that follows is the reader's own with nothing left to the writer
options.misconception: gives the reader everything, which the word collaboration in the sentence explicitly denies

options.text: That readings vary from reader to reader, so the critic's proper work is to collect the range of responses a poem has had rather than to argue between them
options.misconception: makes variation the finding, where the critic is making a claim about how meaning is produced

options.text: That a poem is a script for a performance, so the critic is really describing the conditions under which a reader's account of it is produced at all
options.misconception: substitutes a figure of speech for the claim the sentence is making

questions.explanation: Two words in the critic's sentence carry the position, and the first of them is collaboration, which is a word about joint work and not about either party acting alone. A poem's ending is a thing the text does, a pronoun left without a referent or a sentence stopped short, and it is also a thing a reader does, and what a reader can do with it is bounded by what they bring, which is why a reader who is not unsettled has read a different poem. That last clause is the sharpest part of the claim, and it is not a sneer: it says that the poem's effect is a property of a relation, so two accounts, one of the text and one of the reader, are both necessary and neither is the event. The second option gives the reader everything and abandons the collaboration. The third makes the finding into variation, which is a true and much weaker thing, and the critic is making a claim about how meaning is made. The fourth replaces the claim with a metaphor about performance.
questions.hint: Ask what the word collaboration rules out as well as what it allows.

questions.topic: Two accounts of the same effect
questions.learningObjective: compare a claim about a text with a claim about its readers
questions.stem: One essay says a poem's fourth stanza unsettles a reader by leaving a pronoun without a referent, and calls this a fact about the poem. A second essay describes exactly that feature and calls it a fact about readers of that pronoun in that period. Which comparison is best supported?

options.text: The two are compatible, since the first makes a claim about what the poem does to whoever reads it and the second about what a particular readership brings to it
The first essay is stronger, since a claim about a text can be tested directly while a claim about a readership is a generalisation no reader could check
options.misconception: rests a superiority on testability alone, and a claim about readers is as checkable as a claim about a text

options.text: The two contradict each other, since a poem cannot both unsettle every reader and unsettle only one group of them for reasons of their period
options.misconception: invents a disagreement where there is none, since the two claims are about different sides of one event

options.text: The second essay is stronger, since the same words work differently on different readers and only a historical account can say which effect a poem had at the time
options.misconception: infers a general account from a single group, and it also assumes the two are competing

questions.explanation: The two essays have taken the same feature and asked it two questions, and the questions do not collide. The first asks what the stanza does, and the answer is a description of a text: a pronoun is left without a referent, so a reader is required to supply one or to stop. The second asks what a particular readership supplies, and the answer is a description of a historical situation: readers in one period had conventions about pronouns that made the missing one more, or less, disturbing than it is now. Both are descriptions of the same event from two sides, and a reader who has both knows what the stanza is and what kind of reader the stanza found. The second option ranks the two by testability, and a claim about readers can be tested against the letters, the reviews, and the other poems, which is how a historical argument is conducted. The third manufactures a conflict between a claim about the mechanism and a claim about the audience. The fourth asserts a superiority and then draws a general conclusion from one group, which is the reverse of what an account of that kind can support.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two essays are describing the mechanism or the audience for it.

questions.stem: A critic reads an invented nineteenth-century novel by asking what its language about one country is doing at the moment a reader in another country is imagined to be hearing it. What is the lens being applied?

options.text: The position a text is read from and the position it imagines for its readers, so that an account of elsewhere is examined for what it assumes about whoever is not there to answer
The author's position inside the empire, since a novelist's nationality and circumstances decide what his writing can be expected to see at all in the first place
options.misconception: reduces the lens to a biography, where the question is what a text imagines about the reader it puts outside the frame

options.text: The text's effect on the countries it describes, since a book's doings in the places it writes about are the proper object of a reading organised around empire
options.misconception: moves the question to reception abroad, which is a different enquiry from the one the sentence describes

options.text: The readers the novel actually had, since a serious account of empire should begin with the audience a text was made for and work forward from there
options.misconception: makes reception the starting point, which is a different framework's method rather than this one

questions.explanation: The lens is a question about two positions at once: where the text is written from, and where it imagines the reader to be standing. A novel that describes one country while being read in another is always doing two things at once, and the sentence asks what the two positions produce when they meet, which means that the account of elsewhere is being read for what it takes a reader outside the frame to be. A description that puts people at a distance and an audience somewhere else has an assumption in it, and the assumption is what the reading is looking for. The second option reduces all of this to the author's biography, and a writer's position is one half of the pair. The third turns the question into an effect on the places described, which is reception history. The fourth begins with actual readers, which is a real method, and it is not the one the sentence describes, since the sentence's reader is imagined rather than documented.

questions.topic: A colonial reading that mistakes circulation for agreement
questions.learningObjective: identify what circulation does and does not establish
questions.stem: A critic argues that an invented novel's description of a distant country proves that every reader in the home country agreed with the description, because the novel was published there and sold there. What is the objection to that argument?

options.text: That sale establishes circulation and not agreement, since a reader who bought a book is a reader who was offered a description rather than one who accepted it
That the readers of such a novel cannot be known at all, so no claim about them is possible and the reading ought to be confined to the text itself
options.misconception: denies all reception history, which is a much larger concession than the argument requires

options.text: That a description of a country is not a statement about its readers, so the two have to be argued separately and can never be joined by any argument
options.misconception: denies that a description can be evidence about how it was received, which is the critic's whole claim

options.text: That the sales figures have not been produced, so the claim rests on a number the critic would have to supply and defend in public before it could be used
options.misconception: complains about a missing figure, and the claim does not depend on one since publication and sale are not in dispute

questions.explanation: The argument moves from a fact about distribution to a fact about belief, and the two are joined by nothing. A novel published in a country and sold there establishes that the novel was available to that country's readers in numbers worth a publisher's risk, which is a real historical fact and an interesting one. It does not establish that those readers believed what the novel said about a country they had not seen, and the difference is not a matter of degree: circulation is about the supply of a text and agreement is about what happened in the people who received it, with reading, and not reading, and reading against the grain all inside the same category. The second option is the reaction of somebody who has decided that reception is unknowable, and it gives away more than the critic's argument requires, since letters, libraries, reviews and reprints all make claims about readers checkable. The third denies in advance any link between a text's content and its reception, which would make the critic's own position impossible. The fourth asks for a figure the argument does not need, since nobody disputes that the book was published and sold.

questions.topic: Categories of permission rather than action
questions.learningObjective: state the categories a feminist reading introduces
questions.stem: A critic reads an invented novel by asking which of its characters are permitted to have a career, which are permitted to want one, and which are permitted even to be thought of as wanting one. What categories is the critic introducing?

options.text: Categories of permission rather than of action, so the question is not who does what in the book but who is allowed to be a person who could do it at all
Categories of plot, since a novel's action is what it is about and the critic is reading the book by the way its events are distributed among its people
options.misconception: reduces a question about who may act to a question about what happens, which is the reading the critic is avoiding

options.text: Categories of class, since a character's occupation is settled by money, and a critic who counts careers is therefore counting economic positions of a kind
options.misconception: takes careers as a proxy for money and so turns the critic's questions into questions about economics

options.text: Categories of narration, since who speaks and who is only quoted decides what a novel can be about, and the critic is reading the arrangement of its voices
options.misconception: confuses who speaks with who may act, and a character can be spoken about without being permitted a life of her own

That third question is the one that makes the reading a reading about more than events, and it is why the categories are of permission rather than of action. The second option converts the questions into a count of events and loses the whole point. The third makes careers a stand-in for money, which is a real relation in some novels and not the relation the critic is asking about. The fourth shifts the question to who speaks, which is a genuine feature of a novel and a different question from who is permitted to want something.

B is the better reading, since a count of scenes can be checked in an afternoon and an account of what a reader supplies is an opinion about readers
options.misconception: ranks a checkable count above a reading's significance, which prefers the easier measurement for the wrong reason

options.text: A is the better reading, since a reading about who may act is about the book while a reading about who speaks is about the book's technique
options.misconception: separates a subject from a technique as though a book had one without the other

options.text: The two are rivals, since a novel that withholds a woman's thoughts is a novel whose sympathies are with the men who are given the
options.misconception: makes the two claims rivals when they are the same finding stated from two sides

questions.explanation: The two critics are describing one book from two positions, and there is no point at which their accounts meet in order to disagree. A has noticed that a large part of the novel is occupied by an event the protagonist cannot comment on, and has inferred a withholding; a reader who finishes the book with a strong opinion about the marriage has supplied something the novel declined to give, which is a real and checkable description of how the text works. B has counted the interior scenes by sex and found an asymmetry, which is a description of the book's distribution of consciousness. A reader who accepts both knows that the novel gives a woman's life no interior room and asks a reader to supply one anyway, and those are two halves of one finding. The second option prefers a count because a count is easy, and easiness of measurement says nothing about the size of a claim. The third makes subject and technique separable, and a distribution of interior scenes is both. The fourth makes the two rivals when the evidence of A is the evidence of B, read from a different side.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two critics are describing different features or two sides of one feature.

questions.topic: An intention claim and the evidence offered for it
questions.learningObjective: identify what a claim about a writer's intention rests on
questions.stem: A critic says of an invented novel's epilogue, "The author added it to make the ending less harsh, and a reader who prefers the original ending is preferring a text the author had already given up." What is that claim resting on?

options.text: On an assertion about what the author wanted, where a text's later state is being read as evidence of a purpose rather than as a fact about the text that exists
On a comparison between two printed states of the book, so the evidence is the difference between them and the claim is about which of the two the author stood behind
options.misconception: supplies a comparison between two texts that the claim does not make, since the argument turns on what the author wanted

options.text: On the reader's recollection of an ending that is no longer available, since only a reader who has seen it can say whether the later one is less harsh for being different
options.misconception: makes the evidence a reader's testimony about a harshness the author is supposed to have been aiming at

options.text: On the conventions of the form, because an epilogue is by definition a revision and a reader may take it that any writer who adds one has meant to soften something
options.misconception: grounds the claim in a rule about epilogues, which says nothing whatever about this one

questions.explanation: The claim has two parts and the second is the one doing the work. The critic says the epilogue was added for a reason, and a reason is a fact about a mind, and the only evidence offered for it is that the later text differs from what came before, which is a fact about two states of a book. From a difference between two texts the critic has moved to a purpose in a person, and everything the second part of the sentence depends on follows from that move. The second option is a generous reading and it would make the claim about texts, since a comparison of two printed states is a textual matter, but the claim as made is not that. The third makes the evidence a reader's memory of an earlier text and so makes the case depend on who read which version, which is not what the sentence is doing. The fourth grounds the whole thing in a convention of the form, and a convention can tell a reader that epilogues revise without telling them what this writer was revising for.
questions.hint: Ask what the evidence offered is a fact about, and what the claim is a fact about.

questions.learningObjective: analyse a claim of intention and the reply it invites
questions.stem: A critic says of an invented poem, "The last stanza is ironic throughout, and the poet means it ironically, as his letters show." A reader replies that the last stanza repeats the first with two words changed, and that nothing in the letters mentions irony. What has the reader shown?

options.text: That the letters cannot decide the question, since the evidence offered for an intention is a document about the poet rather than a reading of the stanza the claim is about
That the poem is not ironic, since a change of two words is too slight an alteration to reverse the sense of a stanza that the poet was writing straight
options.misconception: judges an alteration's effect by its size rather than by what the changed words are doing in the stanza

options.text: That the critic's claim is simply false, since a poet who meant irony would have said so in his letters and the letters are the poet's own account of his work
options.misconception: requires poets to document their intentions, which would make the letters the real text and the poem an appendix

options.text: Nothing yet, since a reader's report of what a letter does not say is a negative, and negatives cannot carry the weight of a critical argument at al
options.misconception: rules out negative evidence, when a document that should contain a thing and does not is evidence of a kind

questions.explanation: The reader's reply has two parts and each does a different piece of work. The observation about two changed words is a description of the stanza, and it is the description a claim about irony would have to account for. The observation that the letters do not mention irony is about a document, and it establishes something narrower than it appears to: not that the poet did not mean irony, but that the poet did not say so, so the letters cannot be the ground of the claim as stated. That is enough, because the critic offered the letters as the evidence. What the reader has shown is therefore about the critic's argument rather than about the poem, and the poem's irony is still open. The second option judges the alteration by its size, and two words can reverse a stanza. The third demands self-documentation from poets, and the requirement is what the critic is assuming rather than a fact. The fourth rules out negatives altogether, which would leave a critic free to claim whatever a document happened to omit.
questions.hint: Ask what the letters are evidence of, and what they are being used to prove.

questions.topic: Intention distinguished from what a text does
questions.learningObjective: state the claim that separates intention from a text's workings
questions.stem: A critic distinguishes what a poet intended from what a poem does, and argues that only the second of these is available to a reader. What is the critic claiming?

options.text: That a text's workings can be described without knowing what anyone meant by it, so a reading is an account of a poem and not a report of a mind that stands behind it
That intention is private and uncheckable, so a critic who wants to know what a poem means must give up on meaning and settle for describing the parts instead of them
options.misconception: turns a claim about intention into a claim about meaning, and the two are separate questions

options.text: That an intention is a part of the poem, so a reader who has the letters has one further piece of evidence to weigh beside the images and the syntax of the text
options.misconception: puts intention back inside the text as though a document about a writer were a feature of the poem

options.text: That a poem does what its writer intended, since a poem is the expression of a mind and an expression cannot depart from what is being expressed
options.misconception: denies the distinction the critic has drawn by making the two terms identical

questions.explanation: The distinction the critic draws is a claim about kinds of evidence, and the availability of the second follows from it. What a poem does is a matter of its words and the arrangements they make, and any reader can go and look. What a poet intended is a matter of a person, and the ordinary routes to it, the letters, the biography, the conversation remembered by somebody else, are all reports made by people about a person. So the critic is not denying that intentions exist, and the strongest version of the claim would put it this way: intention may well explain a poem, and there are cases where a letter settles a reading that fifty pages of close attention have not, but a critic who wants to know what a poem is doing does not need to know and cannot be given it by the poem. The second option is a non sequitur, since the unavailability of intention would say nothing about whether a poem means anything. The third puts a document about a writer inside the text. The fourth collapses the two terms the critic has separated.
questions.hint: Ask what the second thing is available for, and why it is available.

questions.topic: Two explanations of one ending
questions.learningObjective: compare an explanation by composition with an explanation by the page
questions.stem: Essay A explains the ending of an invented poem by a change the poet made late in writing it, and says the ending's oddness is what that change left behind. Essay B explains the same ending by the fact that its last line is the poem's only rhyme, and says the ending works by putting a sound where a reader expected a sense. Which comparison is best supported?

options.text: The two explanations are of different things, one a moment of composition and the other a feature of the page, so a reader may accept both without any conflict at all
The two are rivals, since an explanation drawn from composition and one drawn from the page cannot both account for a single oddness in a single line
options.misconception: manufactures an opposition where there is none, since the two accounts are of different aspects of one poem

options.text: The first explanation is the better of the two, since anything that names a moment of composition reaches further into a poem than anything that counts rhymes
options.misconception: asserts a hierarchy of kinds of explanation, which is the thing the pair exists to complicate

options.text: The second explanation is the better, since a claim about the page can be checked by any reader and a claim about composition can only be taken on trust from an archiv
options.misconception: prefers the checkable account and so mistakes a feature of the page for a truer account of a poem

questions.explanation: The two essays are both about the last line and they are answering different questions about it, which is why their conclusions can stand together. A is working on a history: there was a version, the poet altered something, and the ending's strangeness is a residue, so the claim is that the ending looks odd because of something that happened to the poem before the reader got it. B is working on a present fact: this is the only rhyme, so a reader who has been trained by fourteen lines to expect sound to be followed by sense is given sound, and the ending works on that expectation. The two are not competing, and a reader who knows both knows more about the last line than either account gives alone. The second option insists on a conflict where the questions do not meet. The third asserts a depth ranking, and while a residue and a rhyme are different in kind, neither is thereby deeper. The fourth prefers the account a reader can check, and checkability is a property of an account rather than a measure of its truth.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two essays are working on the same object or two objects.

questions.topic: A position on what a writer's account is worth
questions.learningObjective: state the position that an author's account is one reading among others
questions.stem: A critic says that a poet's own account of what a poem meant is no better evidence about that poem than any reader's account, and that a critic who quotes the letters has stopped reading poetry. What is the position?

options.text: That a text is a product rather than a message, so its meanings are made in the reading of it and a writer's testimony is one reader's account standing among others
That a writer is not a person at all, so nothing a person said about a poem can be relevant to it and the letters fall outside any question of meaning entirely
options.misconception: makes a claim about evidence into an impossibility, which produces a position nobody needs to take

options.text: That critics should abandon documentary evidence, so a reading resting on a biography has to be replaced by one resting on the page and the page alone
options.misconception: draws a conclusion about method out of a claim about evidence, and the two are separate matters

options.text: That the author is dead, so reading a poem is an act of mourning and the critic's task becomes the keeping of a maker in memory as a matter of respec
options.misconception: takes a thesis about interpretation and converts it into a duty of feeling toward a person

questions.explanation: What the critic is claiming is about the standing of testimony, and the useful way to state it is that a text is something made rather than something sent, so that it has no addressee whose instructions about it could be recovered. That is what makes a writer's account one account among others: it is a reader's reading like any other, made by somebody with unusual access to the workshop, and access is not the same as accuracy. The second sentence is the sharp end of the claim, because it describes a practice rather than a prohibition, and the practice it names is real, since a critic can spend a career arranging letters around a poem. The second option goes much further and claims nobody may be relevant, which is not what the position says and which nobody would want. The third converts a claim about evidence into a rule about method, and a critic may use documents and still be reading poetry. The fourth turns a thesis about interpretation into a memorial.
questions.hint: Ask whether the claim is about what a text is or about what a writer has ceased to be.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a position on the author does to a reading
questions.learningObjective: explain the consequence and the cost of denying a writer's testimony priority
questions.stem: A critic writes, "I do not want to know what the poet thought he was doing, because the only thing about his thinking I can check is the poem, and the poem is already in front of me." Explain what this position does to the practice of reading, and what it costs a critic who holds it.

answer.exemplar: The sentence is a claim about the order of evidence, and the fact that it is phrased as a preference is a piece of the argument's honesty, since what it rules out is the practice of consulting the letters before the poem. What the position does to reading is to make the text the only thing a critic may describe, so every account of a poem has to be built out of words, arrangements, and the responses they can be shown to produce; that is a productive constraint rather than a poverty, since it is what forces a critic to say which line does which work. The cost falls in a particular and identifiable place. A letter can settle a reading that close attention has not, not because the letter explains the poem but because it records a decision the poem embodies and a reader could not otherwise have guessed at, and a critic holding this position has no way to admit that without giving up the position. What is lost is therefore not the possibility of a good reading but a kind of explanation, the historical one, and with it the ability to say why a line is strange by pointing at a moment when the writer was solving a problem. The example above separates the constraint from the cost, since a position that had no cost would be worth adopting by anyone and the item asks what is being given up.

questions.explanation: An explanation of a critical position has to do two jobs that are easy to confuse: say what the position makes possible and say what it makes impossible, and the second is where an explanation usually stops. The consequence here is a genuine narrowing of method with a genuine gain inside it, and the gain should be named so the position is not dismissed as mere scepticism, because a critic who may only describe a text is a critic who has to say which line is doing which thing. The cost is subtler and has to be identified specifically, and the specific thing is the historical explanation of a local difficulty: a letter that records a writer hesitating over a line is evidence no arrangement of the text can supply, and the position makes it inadmissible. The trap is to write that the position is a method or an attitude, which describes the label rather than the argument, and another is to say it makes criticism harder, which is true of almost any discipline and says nothing about what is here.
questions.hint: Ask what a critic has to do differently, and what one line of evidence is now unusable.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A position that a text's history is a history of uses
questions.learningObjective: state what a position on intention gives up
questions.stem: A critic says that we can no longer share an author's intentions, that we never did, and that a text's history is the sequence of things people have done with it since. What is being given up?

options.text: The idea that a text is about what its author meant, so meaning is something texts have in histories of use rather than something they were sent out carrying
The idea that a text has any history at all, since a claim that intentions are unavailable leaves a critic with nothing but a text's own words to study directly
options.misconception: turns a claim about intentions into a claim about history, denying the very thing the position requires

options.text: The idea that readers have been consistent, since a text's reception has varied so widely that no single account of what it does could hold for all of its readers
options.misconception: concludes from a variety of receptions that texts cannot be read, which is not what the position asserts

options.text: The idea that a text can be read well or badly, since if a text means whatever its readers make of it then every reading is equally a reading of it indeed
options.misconception: dismisses the possibility of a good reading, which is the opposite of what the position is for

questions.explanation: What the position gives up is a particular way of having a history. A text with an intention has one, and it is short, running from a moment of composition to a moment of publication, after which the text's job is to do what it was made to do. A text without one has a history too, and that history is long, made of the readings, the appropriations and the arguments that have been had with it, and none of them is secondary to the others. The first sentence of the critic's account is what buys the second, since a text that was never carrying anything can only have been doing things, and a critic who wants to write about a poem's history is then writing about what has been done to it. The second option is the trap of denying too much: the position needs history, and what it denies is an intention, not a past. The third mistakes a variety of receptions for the impossibility of a good reading. The fourth makes the position into a relativism it does not claim, since a critic can still say that one use of a text has been done badly.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of history a text is left with once intention is removed.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a history of uses does and does not permit
questions.learningObjective: explain what follows for a text's history when intention is set aside
questions.stem: A critic argues, "The letters tell us what one man in one city believed his poems were about, and the way the poems have been used since tells us what the poems have been doing for a hundred and fifty years." Explain what this position does to the history of a text, and what a critic who holds it can no longer do.

answer.exemplar: The position converts a text's history from a story about an origin into a record of uses, and the conversion is visible in the pair of clauses. The first clause is demoted rather than discarded: what one man believed his poems were about becomes a fact of the first decade of the poem's life, a thing that is true of the poems in one city at one moment and is now one item among a very long list. The second clause is promoted, since a hundred and fifty years of use is the part of the history with most in it, and what a poem has been doing is a question with as much to say about it as anything the letters contain. What the critic can no longer do is explain a local feature of a poem by reference to the writer's purpose in it, and the specific case is the odd line. A letter that records a writer trying three versions of a stanza is the best available account of why the surviving one is strange, and this position has no way to admit it without admitting the intention that the letter records, so a critic holding it must find the strangeness in the poem's later life instead, in what readers have made of the line and what the tradition has needed from it. The example above names the demotion, the promotion, and the single lost explanation, since a position described only by what it prefers tells a reader nothing about what it costs.

questions.explanation: An explanation of a position on history has to distinguish what the position keeps from what it relegates, because the common account says only that it prefers later uses, and a position that merely preferred later uses would be a matter of taste rather than an argument. The relegation is the part to name: the letters do not stop being evidence, they stop being the origin of the text's meaning, and they become one dated fact among others. What can no longer be done has to be named as a specific lost operation, and here it is the explanation of a difficulty by a purpose, which is different from explaining a difficulty by a use, since a purpose is settled in one moment and a use is still happening. The trap is to describe the position as a reaction against biography, which is a motive rather than a claim, and another is to say the position is relativist, which is the objection the fourth option in the paired item answers and not the explanation of it.
questions.hint: Ask what has happened to the letters, and what can no longer be explained with them.

questions.topic: Attacking the grounds of a canonical claim
questions.learningObjective: identify what an argument about a canon does to a claim about it
questions.stem: An essay argues that a much-taught nineteenth-century novelist is neither the first nor the greatest writer of the tradition she is said to have founded, and that her reputation was made by two critics and a publisher's list. What has the essay done to the claim that she belongs in the canon?

options.text: It has attacked the grounds of the claim rather than the worth of the works, so a reader is left with a different account of why she is read and not a different judgment of the novels themselves
It has shown that the novels are worse than the novels of the writers it prefers, so the canon is being corrected on the evidence of a comparison between the two sets of books
options.misconception: claims a comparison of worth that evidence about a reputation cannot supply

options.text: It has shown that the novelist is a fiction, since a reputation made by a publisher's list is a reputation with no book standing behind it whatever at the end of the day
options.misconception: turns an account of how a reputation was made into the much larger claim that there is nothing there

options.text: It has shown that the tradition is invented, since a writer cannot found a tradition unless somebody later decides to call her its first member, which is what has happened her
options.misconception: infers that a tradition is unreal because it was made by people rather than by the writers in it

questions.explanation: The essay has done something narrower than it appears to, and the narrowing is what makes the argument good. A canonical claim is a claim about importance, and every such claim rests on grounds, and grounds include not only the works but how they reached the readers who made them important. Two critics and a publisher's list are grounds, and an essay that shows the grounds were selected for reasons other than merit has shown that the claim was never argued for merit at all. What the reader now has is an account of how the novelist became canonical and a set of reasons for doubting the account that was given, and the novels themselves have not been touched. The second option claims a comparison the essay has not made, since comparing novels is a different piece of work. The third makes a much larger assertion than the evidence supports, and an account of a reputation's making is not a demonstration that the reputation rests on nothing. The fourth infers that a tradition is unreal because it was made by people, and every tradition was made by somebody deciding, which is a fact about how canons are built rather than about whether the writers in them are real.
questions.hint: Ask what has been said about the novels and what has been said about how they were read.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Comparative evidence about a canon and its limit
questions.learningObjective: explain what evidence about a canon's making does and does not settle
questions.stem: An essay on a much-taught nineteenth-century novelist sets her beside two contemporaries whose survival in print was arranged by a literary society, and observes that the society chose its list and that her own publisher chose his. Explain how this bears on the claim that she is the important writer of her generation, and why it does not settle the question.

answer.exemplar: The evidence is about the making of a canon rather than about the works in it, and that distinction is exactly what gives the argument its force and its limit. A claim that a writer is important usually reaches its conclusion by a route: the writer's books were bought, reprinted, taught, and discussed, and so the writer matters. The essay breaks into that route and shows that two of the three survivors were put into print by a committee that selected them, which means the survival on which the claim leans was arranged, and arranged by people with interests that need not include the merits of any particular novel. The same observation applies to the publisher's list, and the pairing is what makes the point: a canon made by selectors looks like a canon made by readers. Why the argument does not settle the question is the second half of the explanation and the harder half. A condition of survival is not a verdict on a book, an arranging committee may well have chosen well, and a work that was never printed may be the better novel rather than the equal one. So the essay has removed the warrant for a claim it was never arguing against, and a critic who wants to say this novelist is important still has to say it, and can now say it about the novels rather than about the list. The example above names the route that has been broken, the consequence that the list is not a verdict, and the work that remains.

questions.explanation: An explanation of an argument about a canon has to keep two things apart that the argument deliberately joins: the condition under which a writer was read and the question of what the writer wrote. The join is what makes the essay interesting, because it is the join that a canonical claim normally hides inside the word important, where a large amount of circulation, teaching and reprinting is quietly converted into merit. The explanation should say what the essay has broken, which is the route from survival to importance, and it should be precise that what has been exposed is a condition rather than a falsehood. The second half of the explanation is where the difficulty lies and it must not be softened: an arranging body is not an argument against the books, and a critic who wants to say the essay has proved the novelist unimportant has misunderstood it. The trap is to treat the comparison as settling the question because it feels like a verdict, and the second trap is to treat it as irrelevant because it is only about circumstance.
questions.hint: Ask what route from the books to the word important the essay has interrupted.

questions.learningObjective: explain why a critical method can fail on a particular text
questions.stem: A formalist critic finds a modernist poem of 1922 unreadable and says the poem breaks the relations between form and meaning that a poem is built on, so there is nothing in it for a description to be written about. What is the difficulty with that conclusion?

options.text: The critic has measured the poem by the relations it breaks rather than by the relations it sets up, so the reading fails because the question it asked was the wrong one for this poem
The critic is right, since a poem that breaks the conventions of its form has given a reader nothing that any description could be written about at all
options.misconception: accepts a critic's verdict on a text as a fact about the text, when the verdict is the critic's conclusion

options.text: The modernist poem is the better poem, since the conventions a formalist critic relies on are the ones the twentieth century had already left behind for good
options.misconception: settles the difficulty by ranking two poems, which the critic's conclusion does not require at all

options.text: The critic should read the poem aloud, since a poem that cannot be described on the page can often be heard doing what it is doing when it is sai
options.misconception: prescribes a method rather than repairing a question, and a poem that can be heard can also be described

questions.explanation: A formal reading asks a text to show its relations, and a text that declines to show the ones the critic expected will usually be showing others, which is what happened here and what the critic's conclusion cannot see. The critic has named the failure precisely, that the poem breaks the relation between form and meaning, and has then treated a description of the breaking as the end of the enquiry. But a poem of 1922 that rearranges the relation between form and meaning is doing something with that relation, and the something is available to exactly the kind of description the critic was going to write. The difficulty is therefore not that the poem is thin but that the critic asked what relations the poem keeps and stopped there. The second option accepts a critic's verdict as a fact about a book, which is the confusion the whole discipline is designed to prevent. The third ranks the poems, which the conclusion does not need. The fourth prescribes a reading aloud, which is a method and not an answer to the question of what to ask.
questions.hint: Ask what the poem is doing with the relation the critic says it breaks.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: How far a framework's reach extends
questions.learningObjective: describe the boundary of a critical framework's reach
questions.stem: A historical critic has explained three invented novels of the 1860s by the reform debates they enter into, and a fourth novel of the same decade is left unexplained because none of its characters appears in a pamphlet. What is the fairest account of the method's reach?

options.text: That the method explains a text in proportion to the documents it can attach, so a text with no documentary contact is the one this method has least to say about of all
That the method is mistaken, since a novel that mentions no pamphlet cannot have been produced by a decade of pamphlets and of reform debates in the first place
options.misconception: infers from a text's silence that the conditions the other texts share did not exist, which is a different claim

options.text: That the fourth novel is the important one, since the texts a framework explains least well are usually the ones a tradition has most persistently neglected
options.misconception: infers a value judgment from a method's blind spot, which is a fact about the critic and not about the book

options.text: That the three explained novels are the weak ones, since a novel that needs a pamphlet in order to be understood is a novel that cannot stand by itself at al
options.misconception: turns a difficulty for the critic into a defect in the novels, which reverses the direction of the explanation

questions.explanation: A framework's reach is a fair thing to state, and stating it is what a critic is able to do when one text will not cooperate. The method here works by attaching texts to documents, and a text with no documentary contact offers nothing to attach, so the method has nothing to say about it. That is a boundary of the method and not a verdict on the novel, and the distinction is worth pressing because the fourth novel's silence about pamphlets is a fact about the novel's subject as much as about the decade's records. What the critic can legitimately conclude is that this particular route into the text is closed, and a critic who wants to read the novel will have to find another. The second option uses the text's silence to deny the decade entirely, which would leave the other three novels without an explanation too. The third turns a method's blind spot into a claim about a tradition's valuations. The fourth reverses the direction, treating the critic's difficulty as a defect in three books.
questions.hint: Ask whether the unexplained novel is being judged or the method is being bounded.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Critical terms used without being applied
questions.learningObjective: identify what is wrong with a reading that supplies terms instead of evidence
questions.stem: An essay on an invented novel says, "The text is postcolonial, its narration unreliable, and its gaze deconstructed, and these three facts together account for the reader's difficulty with the second half." What is the objection to that account?

options.text: That the three terms have been named rather than used, since a label applied to a text settles nothing about its second half and the difficulty is left exactly where it was
That the three terms belong to different frameworks, so no single essay may properly use more than one of them and the combination is itself the fault
options.misconception: raises a problem about combining frameworks, when the objection is that the terms explain nothing on their own either

options.text: That a reader's difficulty with a second half is a fact about readers and must be accounted for by a theory of reading rather than a theory of texts
options.misconception: redirects the objection to reception, and the essay's own claim is about what the text is doing

options.text: That the terms are too technical for an essay about a novel, since a reader who cannot supply the vocabulary is entitled to be left untroubled by the text itsel
options.misconception: makes vocabulary an offence against a reader, which is a different complaint from the one the essay invites

questions.explanation: Three terms of this kind are not three pieces of evidence, and the sentence's own grammar gives them away: it treats the names as the facts. A text is not postcolonial in the way it has a page, and the claim is only worth something if a reader can be shown which passage is being described, where in the text the postcolonial condition is doing its work, and what the reading sees that it would not see without the name. The same goes for a deconstructed gaze and for an unreliable narration, and a critic who applies all three to a book without showing one of them at work has supplied a vocabulary rather than a reading. What the essay offers in place of evidence is an account of the reader's difficulty, and the difficulty is exactly what the three terms were supposed to dissolve. The second option is the wrong objection, since combining frameworks is not the problem and the terms fail separately as well. The third turns the essay's claim about a text into a claim about readers. The fourth is an objection to a reader's preparation rather than to the account.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader could point at in the novel that each of the three names is being used to describe.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A reading that never returns to the poem
questions.learningObjective: analyse a critical account that stays inside its own vocabulary
questions.stem: A critic writes of an invented poem, "Its closure is implicated in the discourse of the lyric, so the ending is a crisis of the institution of the poem." A reader asks which words of the poem any of that is about. What has the critic done?

options.text: Supplied a place in a critical system where the poem's own words should have been, so a reader is left holding a position and none of the evidence that would make it a claim about this poem
Answered the reader's question, since critical terms are agreed descriptions of the way poems end and a reader who wants the words is asking too little of a claim
options.misconception: mistakes a critical vocabulary for a shared description, and a term is agreed on rather than agreed about

options.text: Described the poem's language correctly in a technical vocabulary, since closure and discourse are simply the names of the things a close reader would say in plainer words
options.misconception: assumes the terms translate close reading, whereas each of them is a claim that can be wrong about this poem

options.text: Moved the question from the poem to the institution, which is legitimate so long as the critic then goes on to say what the institution is doing to the poe
options.misconception: allows the move it was in the middle of describing, and the difficulty is that the critic never came back

questions.explanation: The reader's question is the only sensible question to ask of a critical sentence, and the fact that it cannot be answered is the finding. Everything in the critic's sentence is a relation between a text and a body of theory, and not one term is anchored to a word of the poem: closure names a general property of endings, the discourse of the lyric names a tradition, and the institution of the poem names a structure that the poem belongs to rather than anything the poem says. What the reader has been given is a position from which a reading might start, and the essay has not started one, so the position has taken the place of the reading it was meant to enable. The second option mistakes a shared vocabulary for a shared account, and critics are agreed on the words rather than on what any of them says about a given poem. The third assumes the terms are plainer speech in a register, when they are claims and each may be true or false here. The fourth permits the move the critic was making and asks only that the critic return to the poem, which is the thing that never happened.
questions.hint: Ask which word of the poem any term in the sentence could be checked against.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A method that produces the anomaly it reports
questions.learningObjective: identify how a rule can generate the irregularity it condemns
questions.stem: A critic reads an invented village chronicle by insisting that every use of the word hundred means exactly one hundred, and then concludes that the chronicle's claims about the size of the village are unreliable. What is the difficulty with that conclusion?

options.text: That the critic's rule decided in advance what a word may mean, so the unreliability belongs to the rule and not to the chronicle's own account of itself
That a word cannot be asked to carry two meanings in any text at all, so the critic's method is the only method and the conclusion holds on that ground
options.misconception: asserts a rule about what words may do, which is the critic's assumption rather than a fact about the language

options.text: That a chronicle is a form that reports numbers accurately as a matter of definition, so any question about its figures is a question about the form and the text itself
options.misconception: takes one convention about a form and applies it to a form that reports in several ways at once

options.text: That a village chronicle was written for readers who already knew the village, so a critic who counts words will always find a discrepancy in a text of this kin
options.misconception: explains the discrepancy by a feature of the audience and so excuses the method that produced the finding

questions.explanation: The critic's finding and the critic's rule are the same thing seen from two sides, and the argument would be sound if the rule were a fact about the language rather than a decision about it. A word like hundred is one of the commonest examples of a term that both counts and suggests, since a chronicle of a village that has grown for four hundred years uses it in both ways, and a reader who has to decide which is meant in a given sentence has a genuine difficulty. What is not open is a rule that decides in advance, because then the irregularity is a fact about the rule and the conclusion that the chronicle is unreliable is a way of reporting the rule's own severity. The second option asserts as a law of language what is in fact the critic's premise. The third applies one convention about one kind of record to a form that reports in more than one way. The fourth explains the discrepancy by the audience, which is an interesting point about the text and does not excuse a method that generated the discrepancy.
questions.hint: Ask whether the irregularity was in the chronicle or in the rule about it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: How a method turns an irregularity into a verdict
questions.learningObjective: explain how a method can generate the anomaly it reports
questions.stem: A critic reads an invented diary by treating every entry as the record of a single day, and then argues that the diarist is lying about her marriage because the two entries she assigns to one evening are dated three days apart. Explain how the reading has reached that conclusion, and what the critic would have to do to make the finding into one that is about the diary.

answer.exemplar: The conclusion follows from the rule in a way the critic never pauses to describe, and the account of the following is the explanation. A critic who fixes one entry to one day has built a grid, and a grid does two things at once: it distributes the entries across days and it leaves a space for a day with two entries on it. The diary has two such entries, so on the critic's grid one of them is misdated, and misdating in a private record read as an account of a life is lying about a marriage, because the whole force of the sentence depends on the fact that a diary is a record of when. But the grid supplied the anomaly, since a diary is a form in which a writer may head a group of pages with one evening, may copy an entry out and lose the date, or may add a page years afterwards and date it wrongly; a grid that allows one entry per day declares all of these to be lies before asking whether the writer had a reason. So the repair is not softer language but a return to the entries, where the critic would have to ask what a writer who put two entries under one evening might have been doing, and to show that a reason exists or that none does. The general point is worth stating, since it is the point the reading exists to illustrate: a method strong enough to make every irregularity impossible has also decided in advance what any irregularity would have meant, and the finding is then a fact about the method. The example above names the grid, the space in it, the reason the space produced a verdict, and the two things a critic must go back and do.

questions.explanation: An explanation of a bad reading has to show the mechanism rather than the mistake, because a mistake described as a mistake teaches nothing. Here the mechanism is the grid, and the explanation has to say what the grid does to the text before it says what the critic concluded from it, because the conclusion is unremarkable and the mechanism is the finding. The second half of the explanation is the constructive one and it must be specific, since saying that the critic should read more carefully is no repair at all; what is needed is a return to the two entries and a question about what the writer might have been doing, with the possibility that the answer is that the writer was careless, which would be a real finding rather than an artefact. The trap is to write that the critic is too rigid, which praises flexibility and names nothing, and a second is to conclude that diaries are unreliable, which is the critic's verdict rather than an account of where it came from.
questions.hint: Ask what the one-entry-per-day rule makes impossible, and what happens to the anomaly it produces.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A shared structure mistaken for a shared condition
questions.learningObjective: identify what most weakens a claim of a universal theme
questions.stem: An essay claims that exile is a universal theme, because a character is exiled in a Greek tragedy, a nineteenth-century novel, and a modern poem. Which observation would weaken that claim most?

options.text: That in two of the three works the exile is the beginning of a return, so what the works share is a shape of plot and the theme has been described as a state rather than a situation
That the three works were written in three languages, so no single reader could judge whether the exiles in them are being described in one sense at all
options.misconception: makes a practical difficulty of translation into the weakness of a claim about the human condition

options.text: That only one of the three is widely read now, so a theme cannot properly be called common when two of its three examples are read by almost nobody today
options.misconception: counts readership as a measure of a theme, which is a fact about circulation and not about what works do

options.text: That exile in the modern poem is a state of mind while in the tragedy it is enforced by law, so the three do not describe one experience and a reader may not call them a theme
options.misconception: offers a qualification a comparative claim is expected to survive and treats it as a refutation

questions.explanation: The strongest observation is the one that shows the three examples sharing something other than what the claim says they share, because that is a problem with the description rather than with the evidence. If exile in two of the three works is the first half of a plot that ends in return, then what the three works have in common is a shape, and a shape can be found in a great many stories without any of them being about exile as a condition of life. The theme has then been described too loosely, and a reader who accepted the claim would be generalising from a plot device. The second option makes a practical problem out of translation, which is a real difficulty for the critic and says nothing about whether the three works share a condition. The third measures a theme by its readership, which is a fact about circulation and tells a reader nothing about what the works are doing. The fourth is a genuine qualification, since a mind and a law are different things, and a comparative claim is expected to survive differences between its examples; it tells a reader to be careful rather than showing the claim is about something else.
questions.hint: Ask what the three works share, as opposed to what the claim says they share.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a formal report leaves for a reader to ask
questions.learningObjective: identify what a formal reading must add after a report of a pattern
questions.stem: A formal reading of an invented sonnet reports that its lines alternate in a pattern the critic can state exactly, and that the pattern is broken at the ninth line, where the line runs long. The reading then stops. What would a reader most reasonably want from it next?

options.text: An account of what the break is doing, since a pattern and its interruption are both facts about the making and the second is only interesting in relation to the first
The sonnet's date, since a pattern of that kind belongs to a moment and a reader cannot place a poem in any way at all without knowing when it was written
options.misconception: asks a formal reading for a date, which is a question about history and not about the poem's making

options.text: A statement of the poet's intention, since a broken measure is a decision and a reader can only judge a decision by knowing what it was made to be for
options.misconception: asks for a writer's account, and so asks the reading to leave the discipline it is working in

options.text: The poem's reputation, since a reading that describes a pattern is a reading of a minor kind of achievement and a reader would want to know what was thought of i
options.misconception: asks for a reception, which is a different kind of question and does not follow from a report of a pattern

questions.explanation: A formal reading is in the middle of a piece of work and has not yet said why it matters. The pattern and the break are both measurements of the making, and a break only becomes a finding when a reader can be told what the poem did with it, since a line running long at the ninth line could be a lapse, a correction of the pattern, or the point at which the poem's subject becomes something the pattern cannot hold. Each of those is a different account of the same measurement, and choosing between them is the work the reading has stopped short of. The second option asks for a date, and dates are the business of a historical reading; a formal reading can be done perfectly well on a text whose date a scholar disputes. The third asks for the writer's account, which is a different discipline and which a formal reading in any case does not need. The fourth asks for a reception, and a reader who wants to know what was thought of the poem is asking about a different subject from the one the reading has entered.
questions.hint: Ask what the reading has measured, and what it has not yet said about it.
